set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: What clinical finding should raise suspicion of coarctation of the aorta?
opts: Unexplained hypokalaemia with resistant hypertension
That combination should prompt screening for primary aldosteronism rather than for a structural aortic lesion.
A marked creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor
This raises concern for bilateral or haemodynamically significant renal artery stenosis rather than coarctation.
Episodic sweating with palpitations and pallor
This pattern suggests pheochromocytoma, where catecholamine release produces paroxysmal symptoms.
Upper-extremity hypertension with weak or delayed femoral pulses
Correct, and the confirmation is to compare arm with leg pressures: normally the leg systolic is the higher of the two, so a reversal of that relationship is the telling finding.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: For which blood pressure categories is lifestyle treatment recommended?
opts: Only once medication has failed
It is a first and continuing intervention rather than a fallback after pharmacological failure.
Only for patients with an identifiable secondary cause
Lifestyle measures apply across the board, including and especially in primary hypertension.
Every category
Correct, which is why an elevated reading that does not yet warrant medication still warrants an intervention, and why lifestyle continues alongside drugs rather than being replaced by them.
Only stage 2 hypertension
Lifestyle treatment is recommended for every blood pressure category rather than reserved for the most severe.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which laboratory clue should prompt a search for a secondary cause?
opts: A normal thyroid-stimulating hormone
A normal result argues against thyroid disease as a contributor rather than prompting further secondary investigation.
Unexplained hypokalaemia
Correct, because it points toward primary aldosteronism. Disproportionate organ damage relative to the blood pressure burden and abnormal renal function are the other two laboratory clues listed.
A mildly raised total cholesterol
Dyslipidaemia coexists with primary hypertension as a risk factor and does not by itself suggest an identifiable secondary cause.
An isolated raised fasting glucose
Insulin resistance accompanies primary hypertension. It is not among the laboratory clues that point toward a secondary cause.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: A patient develops a dry cough on an ACE inhibitor. What is the appropriate response?
opts: Combine the ACE inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker
Dual renin-angiotensin blockade is specifically prohibited because of hyperkalaemia and kidney injury risk.
Stop all antihypertensive therapy
A tolerability problem with one agent is managed by substitution rather than by abandoning treatment.
Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker
Correct. The cough is bradykinin-mediated and occurs in up to about one in five, and angiotensin receptor blockers do not raise bradykinin, so the effect is lost while the therapeutic action is kept.
Add an antitussive and continue the ACE inhibitor
Switching class resolves the mechanism rather than masking the symptom, and an equally effective alternative exists.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: An aldosterone to renin ratio comes back elevated. What is the next step?
opts: Refer to endocrinology for confirmatory testing
Correct. The ratio is a screen rather than a diagnosis, and confirmation plus subtype work belongs to the specialist, which is what determines whether the patient is a surgical candidate.
Start spironolactone and take no further action
A mineralocorticoid antagonist may well be used, but an elevated screen calls for confirmation of the diagnosis rather than treatment alone.
Proceed directly to adrenalectomy
Surgery follows confirmation and subtype determination, since bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism and a unilateral adenoma are managed differently.
Repeat the ratio annually with no other action
An elevated screening result requires confirmation rather than surveillance, because a confirmed diagnosis changes management substantially.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: What dietary and activity targets are described?
opts: Sodium restriction alone, with no activity component
Regular aerobic exercise plus resistance training is described alongside the dietary pattern.
High-protein dieting with unrestricted sodium
The recommended pattern is DASH-style and rich in fruit, vegetables, low-fat dairy and whole grains, with sodium reduced.
Moderate alcohol intake for cardiovascular benefit
Alcohol is limited to low-risk thresholds, and starting alcohol for cardiovascular benefit is specifically not recommended.
A DASH-style pattern with reduced sodium and exercise

Correct, alongside weight reduction, where a sustained loss in the region of five to ten kilograms can meaningfully lower systolic pressure. About 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity plus resistance training is the target.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which patient group is angioedema more common in, and what is the usual substitution?
opts: Patients with asthma, with a beta blocker substituted
Beta blockade is not the substitution for angioedema, and the risk group described is defined differently.
Black patients, with an angiotensin receptor blocker substituted

Correct. It is a class effect of ACE inhibition mediated by bradykinin, and angiotensin receptor blockers can usually be used instead, though angioedema with them remains possible. Angioedema is two to four times more common in this group.
Older women, with a thiazide substituted
Thiazide caution in older adults and particularly women relates to sodium and hyponatraemia rather than to angioedema.
Patients with chronic kidney disease, with a calcium channel blocker substituted
Kidney disease alters the renal and potassium precautions rather than defining the angioedema risk group.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which clinical clues point toward Cushing syndrome in a hypertensive patient?
opts: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations
This cluster is characteristic of pheochromocytoma, in which catecholamine excess produces paroxysmal symptoms.
Loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas
These point toward obstructive sleep apnoea, where intermittent hypoxaemia drives sympathetic tone, rather than to glucocorticoid excess.
Weak femoral pulses with an arm-to-leg pressure difference
These suggest coarctation of the aorta, a structural cause with a quite different presentation.
Proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising and purple striae

Correct, and the width of the striae matters: broad purple striae over a centimetre are what distinguish this from the ordinary stretch marks that accompany weight gain alone. Thin skin and central adiposity complete the picture.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: By how much should mean arterial pressure be reduced in the first hour of a hypertensive emergency?
opts: By no more than about twenty to twenty-five per cent
Correct, with a target around 160/100 to 110 over two to six hours and gradual normalisation over a day or two. Aortic dissection and some stroke syndromes are excepted from this general approach.
To below 130/80 within the first hour
Reducing to the chronic goal within an hour risks ischaemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure, because autoregulation has adapted to the higher pressure.
By at least half, to remove the immediate danger
Overly rapid reduction is specifically harmful. The limit in the first hour is about a fifth to a quarter of the mean arterial pressure.
No reduction until imaging is complete
Stabilisation and controlled reduction begin promptly alongside the focused assessment rather than waiting.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which cerebrovascular events does hypertension predispose to?
opts: Subarachnoid haemorrhage exclusively
The described events are ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage rather than subarachnoid bleeding specifically.
Both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke
Correct. It raises the risk of both mechanisms rather than one, and chronic small-vessel injury separately contributes to white matter change, lacunar infarcts and cognitive decline.
Ischaemic stroke only
Intracerebral haemorrhage is also described, which is part of why sustained systolic burden matters so much.
Intracerebral haemorrhage only
Ischaemic stroke is also described, alongside haemorrhage and chronic small-vessel injury.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: In confirmed resistant hypertension, which fourth agent has the most evidence behind it?
opts: A second dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Adding a second agent of the same class is not among the described steps; the foundational three are titrated first.
Spironolactone, if filtration rate and potassium allow
Correct, and it comes after the diuretic has been optimised and the renin-angiotensin blocker and dihydropyridine titrated to maximally tolerated doses rather than instead of doing so.
A beta blocker
Beta blockade appears among the subsequent escalation options chosen by physiology and comorbidity rather than as the evidence-supported fourth agent.
Hydralazine
Hydralazine is among the later additions and requires combination therapy because of reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: How does initial drug selection differ between stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension?
opts: One agent in stage 1; two complementary agents in stage 2
Correct, and a single-pill combination is preferred where two are started, because adherence is itself one of the main determinants of whether control is achieved.
Two agents in stage 1 and a single agent in stage 2
The escalation runs the other way: more substantially elevated pressure is the reason to begin with two agents.
Lifestyle alone in both stages
Lifestyle applies to every category, but medication is indicated in these stages rather than replacing it.
Four agents from the outset in every stage 2 patient
Two complementary first-line agents are considered when pressure is substantially above goal, not four.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: What is the standard home blood pressure monitoring schedule?
opts: Continuous monitoring for twenty-four hours at home
That describes ambulatory monitoring rather than the home schedule with a validated upper-arm device.
Readings taken only when the patient feels unwell
Symptom-triggered readings would miss the point, since most patients have no reliable blood pressure-related symptoms.
Two readings morning and evening for seven days

Correct, and the instruction not to overreact to the highest single reading is part of it: patients who act on outliers generate anxiety and unnecessary changes in therapy. The two are taken at least a minute apart and the average is reported.
One reading each morning for three days
The described schedule is two readings morning and evening for seven days, which is considerably more data.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: How is resistant hypertension defined?
opts: Severe blood pressure elevation with acute organ injury
That is a hypertensive emergency, which is an acute event. Resistance describes failure of control over time despite adequate treatment.
Above goal despite three complementary drugs at maximal doses

Correct, and each part of that carries weight: three agents, from complementary classes, and at doses the patient actually tolerates. A patient on three drugs at low doses has not yet met the definition.
Blood pressure above goal despite any two medications
Two agents do not meet the definition. Three complementary drugs at maximally tolerated doses are required before the label applies.
Blood pressure that rises again after an initially good response
Loss of previously stable control is a clue that should prompt a search for a secondary cause rather than the definition of resistance.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which pattern of renal artery stenosis predominates in older patients with established vascular disease?
opts: Atherosclerotic stenosis
Correct, and it contrasts with fibromuscular dysplasia, which is an important cause in younger women and is often amenable to percutaneous revascularisation. It is often bilateral and progressive.
Fibromuscular dysplasia
This is the important cause in younger women. It is non-inflammatory and non-atherosclerotic rather than the pattern seen with established vascular disease.
Vasculitis of the renal arteries
Fibromuscular dysplasia is specifically described as non-inflammatory, and vasculitis is not among the patterns named for renal artery stenosis here.
Congenital renal artery hypoplasia
This is not among the described causes. The two named patterns are atherosclerotic disease and fibromuscular dysplasia.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: When is a chest radiograph appropriate in hypertension?
opts: When pulmonary oedema or cardiomegaly is suspected

Correct, and it is explicitly not indicated routinely for uncomplicated hypertension. The principle attached is to order imaging to answer a specific clinical question. A suspected widened mediastinum is the third indication.
Routinely at diagnosis in every hypertensive patient
Routine chest radiography is specifically not indicated for uncomplicated hypertension.
Only to exclude aortic dissection
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude dissection, so it cannot serve that purpose.
Annually for surveillance of cardiac size and shape
No routine surveillance role is described; imaging is ordered to answer a specific question.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: How is obstructive sleep apnoea confirmed once suspected?
opts: Measurement of morning plasma aldosterone
That screens for primary aldosteronism, a different secondary cause with a different clinical picture.
Polysomnography or home sleep apnoea testing
Correct. A positive screening questionnaire raises suspicion but does not establish the diagnosis, and treating the apnoea does not remove the need to continue indicated antihypertensive therapy.
The STOP-BANG questionnaire alone
STOP-BANG is a screening tool. A positive result prompts confirmatory sleep testing rather than establishing the diagnosis by itself.
Overnight blood pressure monitoring
Nocturnal hypertension is a clue that raises suspicion of sleep apnoea rather than a test that confirms it.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: How should the patient be positioned during measurement?
opts: Lying flat with the arm above the head
The arm is supported at heart level with the patient seated and the back supported.
Back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level

Correct, and the instruction not to speak is easily forgotten, yet conversation during the measurement is one of the routine ways an office reading is inflated. The legs stay uncrossed and the patient does not speak.
Legs crossed with the arm resting in the lap
Legs must be uncrossed and the arm supported at heart level, since both departures alter the reading.
Standing, with the arm hanging at the side
Standing readings are taken for specific reasons such as orthostatic symptoms rather than as the standard position.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: What defines a hypertensive emergency?
opts: A systolic pressure above a defined absolute threshold
No absolute numeric cutoff exists for the emergency. Two patients at the same pressure differ entirely depending on whether an organ is being injured at that moment.
Any blood pressure that remains above goal despite three drugs
That describes resistant hypertension, which is a problem of control over time rather than an acute event requiring immediate reduction.
Blood pressure elevation with any symptom, including headache
Headache is common and nonspecific in hypertension. Acute organ injury is what is required, not the presence of a symptom that may be unrelated.
Severe elevation with acute hypertension-mediated organ injury

Correct. The injury defines it rather than the number, and no absolute numeric cutoff exists. A very high pressure with no acute organ involvement is not an emergency, which is the distinction that decides how fast the pressure is brought down.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which substances should a medication review specifically ask about beyond prescribed drugs?
opts: Over-the-counter drugs, licorice and supplements

Correct. Patients frequently do not regard any of these as medicines, so a review confined to the prescription list will miss the cause in exactly the patient whose pressure is otherwise unexplained. Recreational substances belong in the same review.
Only prescribed antihypertensive agents
Confining the review to prescribed antihypertensives would miss the whole category of substances that raise pressure or blunt treatment.
Only agents started within the past week
No such time limit is described, and contributors such as long-term non-steroidal use or oral contraceptives may have been taken for years.
Only intravenous medications given in hospital
The contributors described are overwhelmingly oral and outpatient, including over-the-counter and recreational substances.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: How does obstructive sleep apnoea raise blood pressure?
opts: Autonomous aldosterone secretion
Autonomous aldosterone production is the mechanism of primary aldosteronism and is unrelated to airway obstruction.
Direct mechanical compression of the renal arteries
No mechanical vascular compression is involved. The pathway described is hypoxaemia and arousal driving sympathetic tone.
Intermittent hypoxaemia driving sympathetic activation

Correct, and it explains the characteristic pattern: the pressure is often resistant or specifically nocturnal, because the driver is operating overnight rather than through the day. Recurrent airway obstruction and repeated arousal are what produce it.
Impaired sodium excretion expanding extracellular volume
That is the mechanism in chronic kidney disease rather than in sleep apnoea, which acts through sympathetic activation.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which modifiable factors raise the risk of developing hypertension?
opts: Advancing age, family history and ancestry
These raise risk but are not modifiable, so they inform how closely to screen rather than what to intervene on.
Male sex, independent of anything else
Sex influences risk across the lifespan but is not modifiable, and the described modifiable factors are behavioural and dietary.
A history of childhood streptococcal infection
No such association is described. The modifiable contributors are weight, diet, activity, alcohol and sleep.
Excess weight, high sodium, inactivity and alcohol

Correct, and each maps onto a lifestyle intervention, which is why lifestyle treatment is recommended at every blood pressure category rather than only once medication has begun. Low potassium intake and poor sleep belong on the list too.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: What is the commonest adverse effect of a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker?
opts: Hyperkalaemia
Raised potassium is a concern with renin-angiotensin blockade and mineralocorticoid antagonists rather than with dihydropyridines.
Bradycardia and atrioventricular block
These belong to the non-dihydropyridines, verapamil and diltiazem, which slow nodal conduction.
Dependent ankle oedema
Correct, alongside flushing, headache and gingival enlargement. The oedema follows from arterial vasodilation rather than from fluid overload, which is why a diuretic does not fix it.
Dry cough
Cough is a bradykinin-mediated effect of ACE inhibitors and is not a feature of calcium channel blockade.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which of these is an example of the acute injury that makes severe hypertension an emergency?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram
Hypertrophy is chronic organ damage accumulated over years rather than acute injury occurring now, so it does not by itself make a presentation an emergency.
Albuminuria on a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
Albuminuria marks chronic hypertensive kidney damage and is tracked over time. Acute kidney injury, not established albuminuria, is the emergency finding.
Arteriovenous nicking on fundoscopy
Nicking is a chronic retinal change related to current and previous pressure. Optic disc oedema is the acute finding that indicates emergency injury.
Hypertensive encephalopathy or acute pulmonary oedema

Correct. Brain, lung, kidney, aorta and heart, which is why the assessment of a severely hypertensive patient is a survey of several organs rather than a single test. Any one of them converts a number into an emergency. The full list also includes acute kidney injury, aortic dissection and acute coronary syndrome.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Why might a patient with pheochromocytoma have orthostatic symptoms despite being hypertensive?
opts: Beta blockade has been started first
Isolated beta blockade is dangerous in this condition, but the orthostatic symptoms described arise from volume contraction rather than from treatment.
Concurrent adrenal insufficiency is always present
No such association is described. The explanation given is volume contraction from catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction.
Catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction produces volume contraction

Correct, and it is a genuinely counterintuitive combination: the same catecholamine excess that raises the pressure also shrinks the circulating volume, so the patient is hypertensive and orthostatic at once.
The tumour secretes aldosterone as well as catecholamines
Aldosterone excess is the mechanism of primary aldosteronism, and it would promote volume expansion rather than contraction.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which adverse effects and cautions attach to ACE inhibitors?
opts: Dry cough, hyperkalaemia, creatinine rise and angioedema

Correct. The cough is bradykinin-mediated, which is why switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker usually resolves it while keeping the same therapeutic effect. They are avoided in pregnancy, in prior angioedema and in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
Dependent ankle oedema, flushing and headache
These are effects of the dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers rather than of renin-angiotensin blockade.
Hyperuricaemia precipitating gout
That is a thiazide effect, related to urate handling rather than to angiotensin blockade.
Sedation, dry mouth and rebound hypertension on withdrawal
Those are limitations of the central alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine, whose abrupt withdrawal produces rebound hypertension, rather than of ACE inhibition.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: How may hypertensive heart disease progress?
opts: To heart failure with preserved or reduced ejection fraction
Correct, and both routes are open, which is why a normal ejection fraction on echocardiography does not reassure: preserved-fraction failure is a recognised endpoint of the same process.
Only to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Both preserved and reduced ejection fraction failure are described as possible endpoints, which is why diastolic parameters matter as much as the ejection fraction.
Only to valvular heart disease
Valve disease is not the described progression; the myocardium decompensates into heart failure.
To pericardial effusion and tamponade
Pericardial disease is not among the described consequences of chronic hypertensive pressure overload.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: How should a patient be prepared before blood pressure is measured?
opts: Measure immediately on arrival to capture a realistic reading
A rest period of at least five minutes is specified, and readings taken without it are not comparable to the thresholds used for diagnosis.
Take a single reading to avoid alarming the patient
At least two readings are obtained, with the conditions and any deviation from standard technique documented.
Use any available cuff regardless of arm size
Cuff size must match the measured arm circumference, since the wrong size introduces error into the reading.
Rest quietly for five minutes and empty the bladder

Correct. Technique is not a formality here: getting it wrong is one of the first things to exclude before labelling a patient as resistant, because measurement error mimics true resistance. Smoking, caffeine and vigorous activity are avoided for thirty minutes beforehand.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: By what mechanisms does hypertension accelerate atherosclerosis?
opts: Reduced cardiac output limiting vessel perfusion
Hypertension raises rather than reduces the haemodynamic stress on the vessel wall, which is what initiates the described sequence.
Endothelial shear stress and intimal injury

Correct, and it is why the management principle attached is to treat total cardiovascular risk rather than blood pressure alone, with antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy where indicated. Oxidation of low-density lipoprotein and smooth muscle proliferation follow.
Direct calcification of the arterial media
Calcification is not the described mechanism; the sequence runs from shear stress and intimal injury through lipid oxidation to smooth muscle proliferation.
Immune complex deposition in the vessel wall
No immune mechanism is described. The injury is haemodynamic and then inflammatory and lipid-driven.

set1.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set1.q: Which drug classes are first-line for uncomplicated hypertension?
opts: Spironolactone, clonidine and loop diuretics
Spironolactone is the evidence-supported fourth agent in resistant hypertension, and clonidine is limited by sedation and rebound on withdrawal.
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and beta blockers
That pairing is specifically hazardous because both slow nodal conduction, and neither class is first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
Thiazide diuretics, renin-angiotensin blockers and dihydropyridines

Correct, and beta blockers are deliberately absent from that list: they are reserved for patients whose comorbidities, such as reduced ejection fraction or ischaemic disease, select them. That means ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers among the three.
Beta blockers, thiazide-type diuretics and hydralazine
Beta blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension, and hydralazine is a later addition requiring combination because of reflex tachycardia.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What are the characteristic symptoms of pheochromocytoma?
opts: Snoring, apnoeas and daytime sleepiness
These suggest obstructive sleep apnoea, where the mechanism is intermittent hypoxaemia and arousal.
Flash pulmonary oedema and an abdominal bruit
These are warning features of renovascular disease rather than of a catecholamine-secreting tumour.
The five Ps: pressure, palpitations, pallor and tremor

Correct, and they are typically episodic and highly variable, which is why a normal examination between attacks does nothing to exclude the diagnosis in a patient who describes them. Perspiration is the fifth.
Proximal weakness, bruising, thin skin and purple striae
These are the clues to Cushing syndrome, in which glucocorticoid excess is the driver rather than catecholamines.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What proportion of adults have hypertension by current national survey data?
opts: About one in ten
This substantially understates the burden. Current survey data put adult prevalence at nearly one in two using the 130/80 definition.
About one in four
Still an underestimate. The figure approaches half of all adults once the 130/80 threshold and current treatment are both counted.
Over three quarters
This overstates it. Prevalence approaches half rather than exceeding three quarters.
Close to half
Correct, at 47.7 per cent using the threshold of 130/80 or current antihypertensive treatment. It is the single number that explains why this condition dominates primary care.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which retinal findings relate to CURRENT blood pressure only, rather than to current and previous?
opts: Focal narrowing, haemorrhages and exudates
Correct, while generalised narrowing and nicking relate to both current and previous pressure. The distinction lets the fundus separate what is happening now from what has accumulated.
Generalised narrowing and arteriovenous nicking
These relate to current AND previous blood pressure, which is what makes them a record of the past as well as the present.
Optic disc oedema alone
Disc oedema indicates acute hypertensive injury and marks an emergency rather than belonging to this chronic classification.
Increased arteriolar light reflex alone
An increased light reflex is listed among the chronic changes rather than among the findings tied specifically to current pressure.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: How does alcohol relate to blood pressure?
opts: Excess raises it, and withdrawal can raise it acutely

Correct, and both directions matter clinically: the chronic intake contributes to the baseline, while withdrawal can produce a sudden severe elevation that looks like something else entirely. Withdrawal can produce acute severe hypertension.
Only chronic excess raises it; withdrawal has no effect
Withdrawal is specifically described as capable of producing acute severe hypertension, so the effect is not confined to ongoing intake.
Moderate alcohol should be recommended for cardiovascular benefit
Starting alcohol for cardiovascular benefit is specifically not recommended, and intake is limited to low-risk thresholds.
Alcohol lowers blood pressure and is protective
Excess alcohol raises blood pressure and is listed among the modifiable risk factors for primary hypertension.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What is the first-line imaging test to screen for renal artery stenosis?
opts: Computed tomography angiography in every case
It gives better anatomical detail but is selected according to renal function and contrast tolerance rather than used first in all patients.
Plain abdominal radiography
This is not among the imaging options described and would not demonstrate renal arterial flow or anatomy.
Duplex ultrasound of the renal arteries

Correct, because it screens blood flow without contrast or radiation. Computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography give better anatomical detail and are chosen according to renal function and contrast tolerance.
Catheter renal angiography
This is reserved for selected cases and for planning intervention rather than being used to screen, since it is invasive.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Why must an ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker never be combined?
opts: The two cancel each other out pharmacologically
They act at different points on the same pathway rather than cancelling; the problem is additive harm.
The combination is acceptable if potassium is monitored
The instruction is never to combine them rather than to combine them with monitoring.
Dual blockade raises hyperkalaemia and kidney injury risk
Correct, and the phrasing is absolute rather than cautionary: one is used INSTEAD of the other, which matters because the two look complementary if the mechanism is read loosely.
The combination causes angioedema in most patients
Angioedema is a recognised risk of ACE inhibition specifically. The reason for avoiding the combination is renal and potassium harm without added benefit.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which risk factors are listed for primary hypertension?
opts: Unexplained hypokalaemia with an adrenal mass
These are clues that should prompt screening for primary aldosteronism, which is a secondary cause rather than a risk factor for essential hypertension.
Loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas at night
These point toward obstructive sleep apnoea, a secondary contributor, rather than being risk factors for primary hypertension.
Weak femoral pulses and an arm-to-leg pressure difference
These suggest coarctation of the aorta, which is a structural secondary cause rather than a risk factor.
Advancing age, family history, excess adiposity and high sodium

Correct, and most of them are modifiable, which is the basis for lifestyle treatment being recommended at every blood pressure category rather than only once medication starts. Physical inactivity, excess alcohol, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance complete the list.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What caution applies to thiazides in adults aged sixty-five and over?
opts: Double the dose to overcome reduced renal clearance
No such adjustment is described, and the concern runs toward adverse effects rather than underdosing.
Combine routinely with a beta blocker
That combination is specifically noted to carry a higher risk of new-onset diabetes.
Check sodium, particularly in women

Correct, and it sits alongside the volume status concern in older adults, which is why the monitoring after starting is more than a formality in this group. Those with low-normal sodium or existing hyponatraemia need the same caution.
Avoid them entirely in this age group
A caution with sodium monitoring is described rather than an absolute prohibition.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: How should electrocardiographic voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy be interpreted?
opts: They establish the ejection fraction
Ejection fraction is an echocardiographic measurement; the electrocardiogram assesses rhythm, conduction, prior infarction and hypertrophy criteria.
They are specific but not sensitive
Correct. Meeting the criteria means something, but failing to meet them means very little, which is why echocardiography is used when the clinical suspicion persists.
They are sensitive but not specific
The relationship runs the other way: the criteria are specific but insensitive, so false negatives are common and false positives are not.
They reliably exclude hypertensive heart disease when normal
A normal electrocardiogram specifically does not exclude hypertensive heart disease, which is the practical consequence of poor sensitivity.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which pattern of onset should raise suspicion of a secondary cause?
opts: Early onset, abrupt onset, resistance, or loss of stable control
Correct. All four are departures from the slow, age-related pattern of essential hypertension, and any of them is a reason to look for something driving it rather than simply adding another agent.
Gradual elevation over many years in an older adult
This is the expected pattern of primary hypertension and is the one situation that does not by itself prompt a secondary workup.
Blood pressure that responds well to a single first-line agent
A good response to a single agent is reassuring rather than suspicious, and is the usual course in primary hypertension.
Elevated readings only in the clinic setting
That pattern suggests white coat hypertension, which is addressed with out-of-office monitoring rather than a secondary workup.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which combination must be avoided with verapamil or diltiazem?
opts: A thiazide-type diuretic such as chlorthalidone
No such interaction is described; the combination to avoid is with a beta blocker because both slow nodal conduction.
An angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan
The prohibited pairing in the renin-angiotensin group is an ACE inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than with a non-dihydropyridine.
A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine
The described hazard is with beta blockade rather than between the two calcium channel blocker subclasses.
A beta blocker, because of the risk of severe bradycardia

Correct. Both slow the sinus and atrioventricular nodes, so combining them stacks the same effect, and both are also avoided where the ejection fraction is already reduced. Heart block is the other hazard.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which conditions are named as the common contributors to secondary hypertension?
opts: Coarctation of the aorta and pheochromocytoma alone
Both are genuine secondary causes but they are uncommon. The common contributors are kidney disease, aldosteronism, sleep apnoea, renovascular disease and drugs.
Hyperthyroidism and Cushing syndrome alone
Both cause secondary hypertension but neither is among the commonest contributors, which are led by chronic kidney disease and primary aldosteronism.
Excess dietary sodium and physical inactivity
These are risk factors for primary hypertension rather than identifiable secondary causes.
Kidney disease, aldosteronism, sleep apnoea and drugs

Correct. Knowing the short list is what makes the workup targeted: each has a first test attached to it, so the clues from the history point straight at which test to send. Renovascular disease belongs on that list too.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which symptoms in a hypertensive patient require immediate evaluation?
opts: Confusion, focal deficit, abrupt severe headache or chest pain

Correct. Each maps to an organ under acute injury, which is what converts a high reading into an emergency and changes the timescale of management entirely. Visual disturbance, severe back pain and oliguria belong on the list too.
Any headache at all in a patient with known hypertension
Headache is common and nonspecific. An ABRUPT SEVERE headache is the one that warrants immediate evaluation.
Mild ankle swelling on a calcium channel blocker
Dependent ankle oedema is the commonest adverse effect of a dihydropyridine rather than a feature of emergency.
A dry cough after starting an ACE inhibitor
Cough is a recognised bradykinin-mediated effect prompting a switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than an emergency symptom.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Among adults with hypertension, what does the control figure show?
opts: Control figures are not measured in national surveys
They are measured and reported alongside awareness and treatment, which is what makes the shortfall visible.
Only about one in five reaches the target

Correct, at 20.7 per cent achieving below 130/80. Awareness and treatment figures are both far higher, so the gap is between being treated and being controlled rather than between being ill and being diagnosed.
Most patients reach the target once treated
Treatment and control diverge sharply: about half are treated while only about a fifth are controlled, so treatment does not reliably translate into control.
Control and awareness are approximately equal
Awareness runs close to sixty per cent while control sits near twenty, so the two are far apart rather than comparable.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: In what order must blockade be established before surgery in pheochromocytoma, and why?
opts: Neither is required before surgery
Establishing blockade before operating is exactly what the treatment sequence describes.
Alpha blockade first, then beta blockade
Correct. Blocking beta receptors alone leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, so the pressure can rise sharply. The sequence is the safety point rather than the drug names.
Beta blockade first, then alpha blockade
This is the dangerous order. Isolated beta blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a severe rise in pressure.
Either order, provided both are established before surgery
The order is specified rather than optional, because isolated beta blockade carries a real hazard.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Why is blood pressure measured in both arms at the initial visit?
opts: To average the two arms for the recorded value
The higher consistent reading is used for follow-up rather than an average of the two arms.
To screen for coarctation of the aorta
Coarctation is suggested by comparing ARM with LEG pressures rather than one arm against the other.
Because one arm is always inaccurate
Neither arm is assumed inaccurate; the purpose is to detect a genuine difference and to standardise subsequent measurement.
To find a difference and pick the arm for follow-up
Correct: the higher consistent arm is used subsequently. An asymmetric reading is also one of the examination findings that raises concern for acute aortic pathology.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which study establishes the diagnosis of coarctation, and to whom is the patient referred?
opts: Catheter angiography, with no referral needed
Coarctation requires specialist referral for consideration of intervention, and echocardiography is what establishes the diagnosis.
Echocardiography, with referral to a vascular surgeon

Correct, with computed tomography or magnetic resonance used to confirm. Transcatheter intervention is among the options, which is why the referral is to someone who can offer it. A structural cardiologist is the alternative referral.
Renal duplex ultrasound, with referral to nephrology
Duplex ultrasound screens the renal arteries for stenosis and has no role in establishing an aortic coarctation.
Computed tomography alone, with referral to endocrinology
Cross-sectional imaging confirms rather than establishes the diagnosis, and endocrinology is the referral route for aldosteronism rather than for a structural aortic lesion.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Why does masked hypertension matter?
opts: It only occurs in patients already on treatment
No such restriction is described; the defining feature is the discrepancy between office and out-of-office readings.
It carries real cardiovascular risk despite normal office readings
Correct, and it is the reason out-of-office measurement is not merely a way of avoiding overtreatment: it also finds the patients whose risk the clinic reading conceals.
It is a benign pattern requiring no follow-up
It carries clinically important cardiovascular risk, which is precisely why identifying it matters.
It describes high office readings with normal home readings
That is white coat hypertension. Masked hypertension is the reverse pattern, with normal office and raised out-of-office readings.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What is the treatment goal for blood pressure?
opts: Below 130/80, with lower values encouraged where appropriate
Correct, and the same threshold defines the condition and measures control, which is what makes the national control figure of about one in five directly interpretable.
Below 140/90 for all adults
The stated goal is below 130/80, with encouragement toward lower values where appropriate.
Below 120/80 for every patient without exception
Values closer to 120/80 are encouraged where appropriate rather than mandated for all.
Whatever value the patient tolerates without symptoms
A defined numeric goal of below 130 over 80 is given rather than a purely symptom-guided target, since most patients have no reliable pressure-related symptoms.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What does chronic pressure overload produce in the heart, and why does it matter?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy with impaired diastolic relaxation
Correct, and the word independently is the point: the hypertrophy is not merely a marker of how high the pressure has been, it carries risk of its own beyond the pressure that caused it.
Dilation of the ventricle with reduced ejection fraction from the outset
The initial response to pressure overload is hypertrophy with impaired relaxation. Decompensation to a reduced ejection fraction comes later if at all.
Valvular calcification with progressive stenosis
Valve calcification is an age-related process rather than the described consequence of chronic pressure overload on the myocardium.
Pericardial thickening and constriction
Pericardial disease is not among the described cardiac consequences of hypertension, which centre on hypertrophy and its progression.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: For which features should a patient with renovascular disease be referred early?
opts: Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema or progressive renal decline

Correct. Medical management suits many atherosclerotic lesions, so these three are what mark out the patients in whom revascularisation has the most to offer. Truly refractory control is the third trigger for early referral.
Any degree of renal artery narrowing found on screening
Medical management is appropriate for many atherosclerotic lesions, so the presence of a stenosis alone is not an indication for referral.
A single elevated creatinine measurement
Progressive decline despite optimal medical therapy is the described trigger rather than one abnormal value.
Fibromuscular dysplasia in an older man
Fibromuscular dysplasia is described as a cause in younger women, and the referral triggers are defined by the clinical features listed rather than by that pattern.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Which thiazide-type diuretic is preferred, and what is monitored?
opts: Spironolactone, with renal function monitoring
Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid antagonist valued in resistant hypertension and aldosteronism rather than a first-line thiazide-type diuretic.
Chlorthalidone, with electrolytes and urate monitored

Correct. Hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia are the electrolyte concerns, hyperuricaemia may precipitate gout, and volume depletion matters especially in older adults. Volume status is watched as well, particularly in older adults.
Hydrochlorothiazide, with no monitoring required
Chlorthalidone is the preferred agent, and monitoring of electrolytes, uric acid and volume status is described.
Furosemide, with potassium monitoring only
Loop diuretics are not the described first-line thiazide-type agents for hypertension, and monitoring extends beyond potassium.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What is the initial biochemical test for pheochromocytoma?
opts: The aldosterone to renin ratio
This screens for primary aldosteronism, where aldosterone is high while renin is suppressed, rather than for catecholamine excess.
A low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
This is among the validated tests for Cushing syndrome rather than for pheochromocytoma.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Thyroid-stimulating hormone is the first-line screen for thyroid disease as a secondary contributor, not for a catecholamine-secreting tumour.
Plasma free metanephrines

Correct. Either has high sensitivity, which is what an initial test needs: the priority at this stage is not missing the diagnosis rather than avoiding a false positive. Twenty-four hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are the alternative.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What do most patients with mild to moderate primary hypertension report?
opts: Palpitations and sweating in most cases
That cluster suggests pheochromocytoma rather than the usual presentation of primary hypertension.
No reliable blood pressure-related symptoms
Correct, and headache in particular is common but nonspecific, so it cannot be relied on to indicate the pressure. This is why the diagnosis rests on measurement rather than on how the patient feels.
Headache that reliably tracks the blood pressure
Headache is common but nonspecific, and it is specifically described as an unreliable guide to the pressure.
Visual disturbance in most cases
Visual disturbance is among the symptoms suggesting an emergency requiring immediate evaluation rather than a usual feature.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: Why should not all chronic kidney disease in a hypertensive patient be attributed to blood pressure?
opts: Kidney disease cannot raise blood pressure
It can and does, through impaired sodium excretion and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which is what makes the relationship bidirectional.
Albuminuria is not a marker of kidney damage
Albuminuria is one of the earliest measurable markers of hypertensive kidney damage and is tracked over time.
Other renal causes such as diabetes must be excluded
Correct. Attributing everything to the pressure risks missing a treatable second disease, and the relationship is bidirectional anyway, so the presence of both does not establish which came first.
Hypertension never damages the kidney
It clearly does, injuring renal vessels, glomeruli and interstitium. The caution is about assuming it is the only cause present.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: When is echocardiography appropriate in hypertension?
opts: Only once medication has failed
The indications are clinical findings rather than a treatment failure threshold.
Only to measure blood pressure more accurately
Echocardiography assesses ventricular mass, geometry, function and valves rather than measuring pressure.
Suspected heart failure or a significant murmur

Correct, and it is explicitly not required for every new hypertensive patient. A normal ejection fraction does not exclude preserved-fraction failure, so diastolic parameters and symptoms are read together. Hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram and unexplained dyspnoea are the other indications.
In every newly diagnosed hypertensive patient
It is targeted rather than routine, reserved for the specific indications listed.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What is the standing of beta blockers in uncomplicated hypertension?
opts: The agent of choice in confirmed resistant hypertension
Spironolactone is the most evidence-supported fourth agent in true resistant hypertension.
Not first-line, but preferred in heart failure or ischaemic disease

Correct. The comorbidity rather than the pressure is what selects them, which is the general principle behind individualising antihypertensive therapy. A recent myocardial infarction is the third preferred indication.
First-line for all newly diagnosed hypertension regardless of comorbidity
They are specifically not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension; thiazide-type diuretics, renin-angiotensin blockers and dihydropyridines occupy that position.
Contraindicated in all hypertensive patients
They have defined preferred indications, particularly reduced ejection fraction heart failure and ischaemic disease.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What is the underlying abnormality in primary aldosteronism?
opts: Excess renin driving aldosterone production
Renin-driven aldosterone excess would be a secondary rather than a primary process. In primary aldosteronism the production is independent of renin.
Glucocorticoid excess promoting sodium retention
That is Cushing syndrome, which raises blood pressure through sodium retention and increased vasopressor sensitivity.
Catecholamine excess from an adrenal medullary tumour
That describes pheochromocytoma, which arises from the medulla rather than involving aldosterone from the cortex.
Autonomous aldosterone production independent of renin
Correct, and the autonomy is what the screening test detects: aldosterone is high while renin is suppressed, which is a combination that cannot occur when the system is behaving normally.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What is the caution regarding blood pressure management in acute stroke?
opts: Acute stroke follows a distinct protocol of its own
Correct. Driving the pressure to a chronic target in the acute setting can extend the injury, so the two situations are managed by different rules despite involving the same measurement.
The same targets apply as in chronic prevention
Acute stroke management follows a distinct protocol, and chronic prevention targets should not be applied acutely.
Blood pressure should be lowered as rapidly as possible in all strokes
Rapid reduction risks extending ischaemic injury, and acute stroke is specifically excepted from the general emergency reduction approach.
Blood pressure should be left entirely untreated in acute stroke
A distinct protocol applies rather than no management at all, so the pressure is managed in acute stroke, just by different rules than the chronic ones.

set2.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
set2.q: What does a radial-femoral delay suggest?
opts: Acute aortic dissection
A NEW asymmetric or absent pulse accompanied by pain raises concern for acute aortic pathology, rather than a long-standing radial-femoral delay.
Renal artery stenosis
Renovascular disease is suggested by an abdominal bruit, asymmetric kidneys and flash pulmonary oedema rather than by pulse delay.
Coarctation of the aorta
Correct, and it sits alongside the arm-to-leg pressure comparison as the bedside evidence for a structural obstruction between the two territories.
Peripheral arterial disease
Reduced distal pulses may indicate peripheral arterial disease. A delay between radial and femoral pulses points to coarctation.
